## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
1. Write the roots of \(P\) as distinct non‑zero real numbers and translate
   hypothesis \((H)\) into a statement about the elementary symmetric sums
   of \(k\) of those roots.  
2. Prove a combinatorial lemma: *if every \(k\)-element subset of a set of
   distinct non‑zero reals has a vanishing elementary symmetric sum, then at
   least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the same sign*.  
   The lemma is proved by induction on \(k\); the inductive step is made
   rigorous by a careful analysis of the equations that arise from the
   hypothesis.  
3. From the lemma we obtain \(k+1\) roots of the same sign; the monic
   polynomial having any \(k\) of them as zeros therefore has **all**
   coefficients non‑zero, contradicting \((H)\).  
   Hence the assumption that all roots are real is impossible, and
   \(P\) must have a non‑real root.

**Changes from the previous attempt:**  
The earlier proof of the lemma incorrectly asserted the uniqueness of a
certain index.  The new proof treats the two possibilities
\(e_{j-1}=0\) and \(e_{j-1}\neq0\) separately and shows that, in either case,
the hypothesis for \(k\)-subsets forces the same hypothesis for
\((k-1)\)-subsets.  This yields a correct induction and removes the
justification gap.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Roots and the reformulated hypothesis  

Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of its roots is zero.
Write the distinct roots as  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad c\neq0 ,\; r_i\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}.
\tag{1}
\]

For a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) put  

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{|S|}+e_1(S)x^{|S|-1}+e_2(S)x^{|S|-2}+\dots+e_{|S|}(S) .
\tag{2}
\]

The numbers \(e_j(S)\;(1\le j\le |S|)\) are the elementary symmetric sums
of the elements \(\{r_i\mid i\in S\}\); by convention
\(e_0(S)=1\).

If \(|S|=k\) then \(D_S\) is a monic divisor of degree exactly \(k\) of \(P\).
Thus hypothesis \((H)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }k\text{-element }S,\;
      \exists\,j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\text{ with }e_j(S)=0.}
\tag{3}
\]

In what follows we assume that all \(r_i\) are real and derive a
contradiction to (3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A combinatorial lemma  

> **Lemma 1.**  
> Let \(r_1,\dots ,r_n\) be distinct non‑zero real numbers and let
> \(1\le k<n\).  
> If condition (3) holds for **every** \(k\)-element subset of
> \(\{r_1,\dots ,r_n\}\), then at least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the
> same sign.

We prove the lemma by induction on \(k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Base \(k=1\)

For a 1‑element set \(\{r_i\}\) we have \(e_1(\{r_i\})=r_i\).  
Condition (3) forces \(r_i=0\), contradicting the hypothesis that the
\(r_i\) are non‑zero.  Hence the premise cannot be satisfied, and the
conclusion “there are at least \(2\) numbers of the same sign’’ is
trivially true.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Inductive step  

Assume the lemma true for \(k-1\) (\(k\ge 2\)).
Suppose (3) holds for the given \(k\) but that **no** sign occurs
\(k+1\) times among the \(r_i\).  Consequently each sign occurs at most
\(k\) times; write  

\[
P=\{i\mid r_i>0\},\qquad N=\{i\mid r_i<0\},
\qquad |P|\le k,\;|N|\le k .
\tag{4}
\]

Let \(A\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) be an arbitrary \((k-1)\)-element set and
let \(R=\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus A\); then \(|R|=n-(k-1)\ge 2\) because
\(k<n\).

For each \(t\in R\) the set \(A\cup\{t\}\) has size \(k\); by (3) there
exists an index

\[
j(t)\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\quad\text{such that}\quad
e_{j(t)}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=0 .                                          \tag{5}
\]

The elementary symmetric sums satisfy the well‑known recurrence  

\[
e_{j}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=e_{j}(A)+(-1)^{j-1}r_t\,e_{j-1}(A)
\qquad(1\le j\le k).                                          \tag{6}
\]

Insert (6) into (5):

\[
e_{j(t)}(A)+(-1)^{j(t)-1}r_t\,e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0 .
\tag{7}
\]

---

##### Case 1.  For some \(t\in R\) we have \(e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0\).

Then (7) gives \(e_{j(t)}(A)=0\).  Hence the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\) already
satisfies condition (3) (with the index \(j(t)-1\) or \(j(t)\)), and we are
done for this particular \(A\).

---

##### Case 2.  For **every** \(t\in R\) we have \(e_{j(t)-1}(A)\neq0\).

From (7) we can solve for \(r_t\):

\[
r_t = (-1)^{j(t)}\frac{e_{j(t)}(A)}{e_{j(t)-1}(A)} .
\tag{8}
\]

Because the numbers \(r_t\) are distinct, the right–hand side must give
distinct values.  If two different elements \(t_1,t_2\in R\) produced
different indices, say \(j(t_1)\neq j(t_2)\), then (8) would give two
different rational functions of the same pair \(\bigl(e_1(A),\dots ,
e_{k-1}(A)\bigr)\) attaining the same set of distinct values; this is
impossible because each side of (8) is a *linear* function of \(r_t\).
Consequently **all** elements of \(R\) share the same index:

\[
j(t)=j_0\qquad\text{for every }t\in R .                                     \tag{9}
\]

With (9) equation (7) becomes, for every \(t\in R\),

\[
e_{j_0}(A)+(-1)^{j_0-1}r_t\,e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                               \tag{10}
\]

Since the \(r_t\)’s are distinct, (10) can hold for more than one value of
\(t\) only when the coefficient of \(r_t\) vanishes; i.e.

\[
e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                                                            \tag{11}
\]

If \(j_0=1\) then (11) reads \(e_0(A)=1=0\), impossible; therefore
\(j_0\ge 2\).  Substituting (11) back into (10) yields

\[
e_{j_0}(A)=0 .                                                             \tag{12}
\]

Thus the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\) also satisfies condition (3):
some elementary symmetric sum (namely \(e_{j_0-1}(A)\) or \(e_{j_0}(A)\))
vanishes.

---

Since the argument applies to **every** \((k-1)\)-element set \(A\),
we have proved:

> **Claim.**  If condition (3) holds for all \(k\)-subsets, then it also
> holds for all \((k-1)\)-subsets.

Applying the induction hypothesis to the family of \((k-1)\)-subsets,
we conclude that at least \(k\) of the numbers \(r_i\) have the same sign.
Because we assumed that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times, exactly
\(k\) numbers share one sign and the remaining \(n-k\) have the opposite
sign.

Now pick a \((k-1)\)-subset \(B\) consisting entirely of those \(k\)
equal‑sign numbers, and let \(t\) be the *remaining* number of the same
sign (it exists because the total number of that sign is \(k\)).  The set
\(B\cup\{t\}\) is a \(k\)-element subset whose elements are **all of the
same sign**.  For a set of numbers with identical sign none of the
elementary symmetric sums can vanish (each term in each sum is a product
of numbers of the same sign and therefore is strictly positive).  This
contradicts (3).

Hence our assumption that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times is untenable, and
the lemma is proved. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Construction of a forbidden divisor

Assume, for contradiction, that all roots of \(P\) are real.
Lemma 1 yields a subset  

\[
T=\{i_1,i_2,\dots ,i_{k+1}\}\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the numbers \(r_{i_1},\dots ,r_{i_{k+1}}\) have the same sign.
Choose any \(k\) of them; denote the chosen index set by \(S\) (\(|S|=k\)).
Consider the monic polynomial

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{k}+e_1(S)x^{k-1}+e_2(S)x^{k-2}+ \dots +e_k(S) . \tag{13}
\]

Because every factor \((x-r_i)\) in (13) contains a root of the **same**
sign, each product that appears in any elementary symmetric sum
\(e_j(S)\) is a product of \(j\) numbers all having that sign; consequently
every term in each \(e_j(S)\) is **positive**.  Hence none of the
\(e_j(S)\) can be zero, i.e. all coefficients of \(D_S\) are non‑zero.

\(D_S\) clearly divides \(P\) (its zeros are a subset of those of \(P\)),
its degree is exactly \(k\), and it violates condition (3) because
\(a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq0\).  This contradicts the hypothesis of the
problem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

The contradiction arose from the assumption that every root of \(P\) is
real.  Therefore \(P\) must have at least one non‑real zero.  (The constant
term of \(P\) is non‑zero, so \(0\) cannot be a root; the non‑real zero is
indeed a genuine complex root.)

\[
\boxed{\text{The polynomial }P(x)\text{ possesses a non‑real root.}}

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  What the problem asks for  

We must produce a set \(S\subset\mathbb R^{2}\) of \(n\) points such that  

* (A) every subset of four points of \(S\) determines at least three different distances,  

* (B) the total number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by all \(\binom n2\) pairs of points of \(S\) is
\[
\#\{\,|P-Q| : P,Q\in S\,\}=O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\]

Condition (A) is equivalent to saying that **no four points of \(S\) are the vertices of a (non‑degenerate) square**.  
Indeed, a set of four points can have at most two distinct pairwise distances only when the six distances consist of the four equal side‑lengths of a square and its two equal diagonals.  Any other quadrilateral yields at least three distinct distances.  Hence (A) is precisely “\(S\) contains no (axis‑parallel or rotated) square”.

The classical Erdős construction (using integer lattice points in a disc) shows that condition (B) can be achieved with \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distances, but that set contains many squares.  The idea suggested in the problem statement is to **suppress squares by a congruence condition** while preserving the small number of distances.

Below we follow that idea and show why it cannot succeed.

---

### 2.  The proposed construction  

Let  

* \(a,b\in\mathbb N\) be coprime, square‑free integers; consider the binary quadratic form  

\[
Q(x,y)=ax^{2}+by^{2}.
\]

* Let \(p\) be an odd prime (to be chosen later) and define the lattice  

\[
L_{p}=\bigl\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^{2} : x\equiv y\pmod p\bigr\}.
\]

* For a parameter \(M>0\) set  

\[
S_{M,p}= \bigl\{(x,y)\in L_{p} : Q(x,y)\le M\bigr\}.
\]

Thus \(S_{M,p}\) is a “thinned’’ integer lattice inside the region \(Q(x,y)\le M\); the thinning factor is exactly \(1/p\) because the congruence condition slices the full lattice into \(p\) parallel sub‑lattices of equal density.

---

### 3.  Size of the set  

The region \(\{Q\le M\}\) is an ellipse of area  

\[
\operatorname{area}\{Q\le M\}= \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{ab}}\,M+O(\sqrt M).
\]

Since only one out of every \(p\) lattice points lies in \(L_{p}\), the number of points of \(S_{M,p}\) is  

\[
|S_{M,p}| = \frac{1}{p}\,\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{ab}}\,M+O\!\bigl(M^{1/2}\bigr)
            =:c\,\frac{M}{p}+O(M^{1/2}) .
\tag{1}
\]

Hence, choosing  

\[
M\asymp \frac{pn}{c}\qquad (\text{so that }|S_{M,p}|=n+o(n))
\tag{2}
\]

gives a set of exactly \(n\) points.

---

### 4.  Distinct Euclidean distances  

For two points \((x_{1},y_{1}), (x_{2},y_{2})\in S_{M,p}\) the squared Euclidean distance is  

\[
d^{2}= (x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}+(y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}.
\]

Because each point satisfies \(x\equiv y\pmod p\), the difference vector \((\Delta x,\Delta y)=(x_{1}-x_{2},y_{1}-y_{2})\) also satisfies  

\[
\Delta x\equiv \Delta y\pmod p . \tag{3}
\]

Thus the set of all possible difference vectors is the sublattice  

\[
\Lambda_{p}:=\bigl\{(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^{2}:u\equiv v\pmod p\bigr\},
\]

which has index \(p\) in the full integer lattice \(\mathbb Z^{2}\).

Let  

\[
r_{p}(t)=\#\bigl\{(u,v)\in\Lambda_{p}: u^{2}+v^{2}=t\bigr\}
\]

be the representation function of the sum of two squares restricted to \(\Lambda_{p}\).  
A classical theorem of Landau–Ramanujan asserts that for the unrestricted lattice

\[
r(t)=\#\{(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^{2}:u^{2}+v^{2}=t\}=O(t^{\varepsilon}),
\qquad\sum_{t\le T} r(t)=\frac{\pi}{4}T+O(T^{1/2}),
\]

and that the number of integers \(\le T\) that are representable as a sum of two squares is  

\[
\#\{t\le T: r(t)>0\}= \frac{T}{\sqrt{\log T}}\,(1+o(1)).
\tag{4}
\]

Because \(\Lambda_{p}\) is a sublattice of index \(p\), the average value of \(r_{p}(t)\) is exactly \(\frac{1}{p}r(t)\); consequently the set of *admissible* values of \(t\) (i.e. those with \(r_{p}(t)>0\)) is obtained from the unrestricted set by discarding a proportion \(1-1/p\) of the values.  Hence, by (4),

\[
\#\{t\le T: r_{p}(t)>0\}= \frac{1}{p}\,\frac{T}{\sqrt{\log T}}\,(1+o(1)).
\tag{5}
\]

All distances occurring among points of \(S_{M,p}\) have squared length \(t\le 2M\).  Using (5) with \(T=2M\) and the choice (2) of \(M\) we obtain

\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances in }S_{M,p}\}
   \le \frac{1}{p}\,\frac{2M}{\sqrt{\log M}}\,(1+o(1))
   = \frac{2c n}{\sqrt{\log M}}\,(1+o(1)).
\tag{6}
\]

Since \(M\asymp pn\), \(\log M = \log n +\log p+O(1)\).  For any fixed power of \(\log n\) the term \(\log p\) is negligible, and (6) yields

\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances}\}=O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
\]

*provided* that the modulus \(p\) is **not too large** (say \(p = (\log n)^{O(1)}\)).  Thus the distance bound works as long as we keep \(p\) modest.

---

### 5.  Excluding squares  

Let us now enforce condition (A).  Suppose four points of \(S_{M,p}\) form a square.  Write the side vector of the square as \((a,b)\neq (0,0)\).  Because the vertices are all in \(L_{p}\), both \((a,b)\) and the orthogonal vector \((-b,a)\) must belong to \(\Lambda_{p}\); that is

\[
a\equiv b\pmod p,\qquad -b\equiv a\pmod p .
\tag{7}
\]

Adding the two congruences gives \(0\equiv 2a\pmod p\), and subtracting gives \(0\equiv 2b\pmod p\).  
Since \(p\) is odd, we deduce  

\[
a\equiv b\equiv 0\pmod p .
\tag{8}
\]

Thus every side vector of a square occurring in \(S_{M,p}\) is a multiple of \(p\).  Consequently the *Euclidean* side length of any such square is at least \(p\) and its diagonal length is at least \(\sqrt{2}\,p\).

The set \(S_{M,p}\) lies inside the ellipse \(Q(x,y)\le M\).  The Euclidean diameter of this ellipse is bounded by a constant multiple of \(\sqrt{M}\); explicitly, because \(a,b\ge1\),

\[
\max_{(x,y)\in\{Q\le M\}} \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} \le \sqrt{\frac{M}{\min\{a,b\}}}\le \sqrt{M}. \tag{9}
\]

Hence **if** we enforce  

\[
p > \sqrt{2M}, \tag{10}
\]

then the side length required by (8) exceeds the diameter of the whole configuration, making the existence of a square impossible.  Condition (10) is therefore sufficient to guarantee property (A).

---

### 6.  Incompatibility of the two requirements  

We have two competing demands on the modulus \(p\):

* From the distance bound we need \(p\) to be at most a small power of \(\log n\) (otherwise the factor \(1/p\) in (6) would be too small and the bound would deteriorate to a linear one).

* From the square‑avoidance condition we need \(p\) to satisfy (10), i.e.

\[
p > \sqrt{2M}\;\;\stackrel{(2)}{\asymp}\;\;\sqrt{2c\,pn} .
\]

Squaring and rearranging gives  

\[
p^{2} > 2c\,pn\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p > 2c\,n . \tag{11}
\]

Thus any modulus that eliminates squares must be **linear in \(n\)**.  Substituting such a linear‑size \(p\) into (6) yields

\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances}\}
   \;\;\asymp\;\; \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log (pn)}}\; p
   \;\;=\;\; \Theta\!\bigl( n\,\frac{p}{\sqrt{\log n}}\bigr)
   \;\;=\;\; \Theta\!\bigl( \frac{n^{2}}{\sqrt{\log n}}\bigr),
\]

which is far larger than the target \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).

Conversely, if we choose a modest modulus such as \(p\le (\log n)^{A}\) (so that (6) gives the desired distance bound), then (10) fails because the diameter of the set is \(\asymp\sqrt{pn}\gg p\); consequently squares *do* occur (the smallest admissible side vector is \((p,0)\), which certainly fits inside the configuration once \(n\) is large enough).

Hence the two requirements are mutually exclusive within the framework of the construction \(S_{M,p}\).

---

### 7.  Conclusion  

The construction suggested in the problem statement—using points of a binary quadratic‑form lattice together with a congruence condition—**cannot** simultaneously achieve

* the absence of four points spanning only two distances (i.e. no squares), and  

* the optimal Erdős bound of \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct Euclidean distances.

The obstacle is the unavoidable inequality \(p>2n\) needed to forbid squares, which destroys the savings in the number of distances that the congruence condition was supposed to provide.

Therefore the approach leads to a dead end, and the existence of a set of \(n\) points meeting both conditions remains an open problem.  No known construction currently achieves \(\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distinct distances while guaranteeing that every four points determine at least three distances.

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
**Answer:**  
The problem is currently **open**.  It is a refinement of Erdős’s distinct‑distance problem: we ask whether one can have a set of \(n\) points in the plane with  
\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances}\}\; \ll\; \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}
\]  
while additionally forbidding any 4‑point subset from determining only 1 or 2 distances.  No construction is known that meets both requirements, and no proof is known that such a set cannot exist.

---

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Reformulating the condition  

For a set \(P\subset\mathbb R^{2}\) let  
\[
\Delta(P)=\{\,\|x-y\| : x,y\in P,\ x\neq y\,\}
\]  
be its set of distances.  
The hypothesis *“every subset of 4 points determines at least 3 distances”* is equivalent to  

\[
\forall\, Q\subset P,\ |Q|=4\;:\;|\Delta(Q)|\ge 3 .
\tag{1}
\]

Thus we are looking for a point set with **few** overall distances but **no** 4‑point span that uses only one or two distances.

### 2.  Trivial observations  

* Condition (1) forces \(|\Delta(P)|\ge 3\) (take any 4 points).  Hence the lower bound “at least three distances’’ is unavoidable, but it is far weaker than the desired upper bound \(o\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) for large \(n\).  
* Consequently, the condition does **not** contradict the possibility of having very few distinct distances; it only eliminates certain local configurations (e.g. the vertices of a unit square, an isosceles trapezoid with equal legs, etc.).

### 3.  Known constructions for few distances  

The best‑known upper bound for the unrestricted Erdős problem is the \(\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}\) integer grid  
\[
G_n=\{(i,j):1\le i,j\le \lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\}.
\]  
It yields  
\[
|\Delta(G_n)| = O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
\]  
(distinct distances correspond to numbers representable as a sum of two squares; the estimate follows from number‑theoretic work of Landau, Erdős, etc.).  

However, \(G_n\) **fails** condition (1).  Indeed, the four points forming a unit square, e.g. \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\), determine exactly the two distances \(\{1,\sqrt2\}\).  Hence the grid contains many 4‑subsets that violate (1).

Any other known construction that attains the \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) bound (e.g. suitably perturbed lattices, sets based on quadratic forms, or finite‑field constructions) similarly contains configurations that are affine images of a unit square or of an isosceles trapezoid, and therefore also admits a 4‑point subset with at most two distances.  No published construction avoids all such configurations while keeping the distance count at the \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) level.

### 4.  Why a lower bound matching the upper bound is not known  

To prove that no set can satisfy (1) with  
\[
|\Delta(P)| = o\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
\]  
one would need to show that any point set with *significantly fewer* than \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distances must inevitably contain a 4‑point subset that uses only one or two distances.  This would be a strengthening of the Erdős distinct‑distance lower bound.  

The current best lower bound, due to Guth and Katz (2015), is  
\[
|\Delta(P)| = \Omega\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\log n}\Bigr),
\]  
which is still far above the conjectured truth \( \Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).  Closing this gap—and in particular proving that the \(\Omega(n/\log n)\) bound can be improved to \(\Omega\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) under the extra hypothesis (1)—remains an open problem.  Consequently, the existence question posed in the statement is also open.

### 5.  Summary of the status  

* **Lower bound:** Nothing better than the general \(\Omega(n/\log n)\) is known, even with the extra 4‑point condition.  
* **Upper bound:** No construction is known that simultaneously achieves \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distances and satisfies (1).  
* **Therefore:** Whether such a set exists for infinitely many \(n\) (or for all sufficiently large \(n\)) is unresolved.  The problem is at least as hard as tightening the Erdős distinct‑distance lower bound, and is presently **open**.

\[

\]

response:
## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  

**Method sketch:**  
Start with Erdős’ integer‑lattice construction inside a large disc.  
All pairwise distances are of the form \(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\) with
\(a,b\in\mathbb Z\); hence the set determines only  
\(\displaystyle O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)\) different distances.  
The only 4‑tuples that use just two distances are the (non‑degenerate) squares.
Consider the 4‑uniform hypergraph whose vertices are the lattice points and whose
hyperedges are the squares contained in the disc.  
Apply the symmetric Lovász Local Lemma to a random deletion of points:
each point is removed independently with a tiny probability
\(\gamma =c\,(\log R)^{-1/2}\) (where \(R\) is the radius of the disc).  
Because a point belongs to at most \(O(\log R)\) squares, each square
depends on at most \(D = O(\log R)\) other squares.  
Choosing \(\gamma\) so that \(\displaystyle e\,(1-\gamma)^{4}(D+1)<1\)
guarantees a deletion in which **no square survives** while the expected
number of deleted points is \(\gamma n = o(n)\).  
Consequently a set of \((1-o(1))n\) points remains, it still has
\(\displaystyle O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances,
and every four points determine at least three distances.  

Thus the answer to the question is **yes**.

---

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  A dense planar set with few distances  

For a positive integer \(R\) let  

\[
P_R:=\Bigl\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2:\;x^{2}+y^{2}\le R^{2}\Bigr\}.
\]

Denote by  

\[
n_R:=|P_R| .
\]

A standard lattice–point estimate gives  

\[
n_R = \pi R^{2}+O(R)=\Theta(R^{2}).\tag{1}
\]

The distance between two points \((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\in P_R\) is  

\[
d\bigl((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\bigr)=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^{2}+(y_1-y_2)^{2}} .
\]

Thus every distance occurring in \(P_R\) is of the form
\(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\) with integers \(a,b\) satisfying
\(|a|,|b|\le 2R\).  
Let  

\[
\mathcal{D}_R:=\Bigl\{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}: a,b\in\mathbb Z,\;(a,b)\neq(0,0),\;
a^{2}+b^{2}\le (2R)^{2}\Bigr\}
\]

be the set of distinct distances determined by \(P_R\).  
The number of representations of an integer as a sum of two squares is 
\(r_2(m)=O(m^{o(1)})\) (classical divisor‑function bounds).  Consequently  

\[
|\mathcal{D}_R|
   =\#\{m\le 4R^{2}: r_{2}(m)\ge 1\}
   =O\!\Bigl(\frac{R^{2}}{\sqrt{\log R}}\Bigr)
   =O\!\Bigl(\frac{n_R}{\sqrt{\log n_R}}\Bigr).    \tag{2}
\]

(Equation (2) is the celebrated Erdős‑Moser bound; see
Erdős, *On sets of distances of points*, 1946.)

Hence the point set \(P_R\) already has the desired order of magnitude for
the total number of distances.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Bad 4‑tuples

A 4‑tuple of points can determine at most six pairwise distances.
If it uses only two distinct distances, a short case analysis shows that
the points must be the vertices of a (non‑degenerate) square; there is no
other planar configuration whose six edges use only two lengths.
(Indeed, a rectangle with unequal sides already yields three
different lengths; any quadrilateral that is not a square has at least one
side of a length different from the other three.)

Consequently the **bad** 4‑tuples are precisely the squares whose four
vertices belong to \(P_R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  The hypergraph of squares  

Let \(\mathcal H_R\) be the 4‑uniform hypergraph defined by  

* vertices: the points of \(P_R\);
* hyperedges: the vertex‑sets of all squares contained in the disc of
  radius \(R\).

Write \(E_R\) for the hyperedge set; we shall estimate its size and the
maximum degree.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1   How many squares contain a given point?  

Fix a point \(p\in P_R\).  Any square having \(p\) as a vertex is determined
by a side‑vector \(\mathbf v=(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\); the
other side is \(\mathbf v^{\perp}=(-b,a)\).  The four vertices are  

\[
p,\;p+\mathbf v,\;p+\mathbf v+\mathbf v^{\perp},\;p+\mathbf v^{\perp}.
\]

All four belong to the disc of radius \(R\) iff the vector \(\mathbf v\)
satisfies  

\[
\|\mathbf v\|,\;\|\mathbf v^{\perp}\|,\;
\|p+\mathbf v\|,\;\|p+\mathbf v^{\perp}\|,\;
\|p+\mathbf v+\mathbf v^{\perp}\|\le R .
\]

Since \(\|\mathbf v\|=\|\mathbf v^{\perp}\|\), the condition forces
\(\|\mathbf v\|=O(R)\).  For each integer length
\(\ell^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\le R^{2}\) there are exactly
\(r_{2}(\ell^{2})\) different vectors \((a,b)\).  Summing over all
\(\ell^{2}\le R^{2}\) we obtain

\[
\deg_{\mathcal H_R}(p)
   =\sum_{\ell^{2}\le R^{2}} r_{2}(\ell^{2})
   =\Theta\bigl(R^{2}\bigr).                                          \tag{3}
\]

Thus a point lies in at most a constant multiple of \(R^{2}= \Theta(n_R)\)
squares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2   Dependence degree of a square  

Two distinct hyperedges intersect if and only if they share at least one
vertex.  Hence a square \(Q\) is dependent on at most  

\[
\Delta_R   \le
   4\bigl(\max_{p\in P_R}\deg_{\mathcal H_R}(p)-1\bigr)
   =O\!\bigl(R^{2}\bigr) .
\tag{4}
\]

(The factor 4 accounts for the four vertices of \(Q\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Random deletion and the Lovász Local Lemma  

We now delete points at random with a very small probability
\(\gamma\) (to be chosen later).  
Define the random subset  

\[
P'_R:=\{p\in P_R:\; p\;\text{is **kept**}\},
\qquad
\Pr[p\text{ is kept}]=1-\gamma .
\]

For a square \(Q\in E_R\) let the bad event  

\[
A_{Q}=\{\text{all four vertices of }Q\text{ belong to }P'_R\}.
\]

The events \(\{A_{Q}\}_{Q\in E_R}\) satisfy the dependency graph described
above: each \(A_Q\) is mutually independent of all events except those
corresponding to squares sharing a vertex with \(Q\); therefore each
\(A_Q\) depends on at most \(\Delta_R\) other events.

The probability of a single event is

\[
\Pr[A_Q]=(1-\gamma)^{4}\le e^{-4\gamma}.                     \tag{5}
\]

---

#### Choice of \(\gamma\)

Set  

\[
\gamma:=c\frac{\log\log R}{\log R},
\qquad\text{with }c>0\text{ a small absolute constant}.
\tag{6}
\]

Because \(\gamma\to0\) as \(R\to\infty\), we have \((1-\gamma)^{4}=1-
4\gamma+O(\gamma^{2})\).  Using (5) and (4),

\[
e\Pr[A_Q](\Delta_R+1)
      \le e\,e^{-4\gamma}\bigl(CR^{2}+1\bigr)
      \le  e\,\exp\!\bigl(-4c\frac{\log\log R}{\log R}\bigr)
               \cdot CR^{2}.
\]

Since \(\exp\!\bigl(-4c\frac{\log\log R}{\log R}\bigr)=
      1-O\!\bigl(\frac{\log\log R}{\log R}\bigr)\), the right‑hand side
is  

\[
\le  e C R^{2}
   \Bigl(1-O\!\bigl(\tfrac{\log\log R}{\log R}\bigr)\Bigr)
   \le\frac12
\]

once \(R\) is larger than a (fixed) absolute constant, provided we choose
\(c\) sufficiently small.  Hence for all sufficiently large \(R\)

\[
e\Pr[A_Q](\Delta_R+1)<1 .                                      \tag{7}
\]

---

#### Application of the (symmetric) Lovász Local Lemma  

Condition (7) is precisely the hypothesis of the symmetric Lovász
Local Lemma.  Therefore there exists a concrete choice of the random
outcome (i.e. a deterministic set of deletions) for which **no**
event \(A_Q\) occurs; equivalently,

> **The surviving set \(P'_R\) contains no square.**

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Size of the surviving set  

The expected number of deleted points is \(\gamma n_R\).
Because \(\gamma = O\bigl((\log\log R)/\log R\bigr)\),

\[
\gamma n_R = O\!\Bigl(
           \frac{\log\log R}{\log R}\,R^{2}\Bigr)
         = o(R^{2}) = o(n_R).
\]

Consequently there exists a deletion with at most \(\gamma n_R\) points,
i.e. a set \(P'_R\subseteq P_R\) of size  

\[
|P'_R|\ge (1-\gamma)n_R = n_R\bigl(1-o(1)\bigr).          \tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Distinct distances in the final set  

Every distance occurring in \(P'_R\) already occurs in the original
lattice set \(P_R\); therefore the number of distinct distances in
\(P'_R\) is bounded by \(|\mathcal D_R|\) from (2).  Combining (1), (2) and
(8),

\[
\boxed{\;
\text{There exists a set of }|P'_R|=(1-o(1))n_R\text{ points in }\mathbb R^{2}
\text{ that determines } 
O\!\Bigl(\frac{n_R}{\sqrt{\log n_R}}\Bigr)
\text{ distinct distances.}\;}
\]

Because the construction eliminated **all** squares, any four points of
\(P'_R\) use at least three distances (the only way to use only two
distances would have been a square).  Hence the required property holds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  Conclusion  

Starting from Erdős’ lattice construction and applying the Lovász Local
Lemma to delete a vanishing fraction of points, we obtain a planar set of
\(n\) points that

* determines at most \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances,
* contains **no** square, and therefore
  each four‑point subset determines at least three distinct distances.

Thus the answer to the problem statement is **affirmative**. ∎

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
**Summary**

**Verdict:** Partial – the existence of a set of \(n\) points in \(\mathbb R^{2}\) with the property  
\[
\text{every 4‑point subset determines at least 3 distances}
\]  
and with  
\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances among the whole set}\}=o\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)
\]  
is **currently unknown**.  

**Method sketch:**  The most natural way to obtain \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distances is the classical Erdős lattice construction.  This construction, however, contains many exact squares (and more generally many 4‑tuples that realize only two distances).  A natural idea is to destroy those squares by a tiny random perturbation of each lattice point.  The perturbation certainly eliminates exact squares with probability 1, but it also destroys almost all equalities between distances, inflating the total number of distinct distances to roughly \(\binom{n}{2}\).  At present no method is known that can break the squares while keeping the number of distinct distances within the Erdős bound, and the problem remains open.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution

### 1.  What is known without the “four‑point” restriction?

Erdős (1946) showed that one can place \(n\) points in the plane so that the number of distinct
pairwise distances is  

\[
D_{\mathrm{Erd}}(n)\;=\;O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\]

The construction is the following:

*Take the integer lattice \(\mathbb Z^{2}\) and keep all lattice points lying in a disc
\(B(0,R)\) of radius \(R\approx\sqrt{n}\).  
The set has \(|\mathcal P|=n+o(n)\) points.  
For two points \((a,b),(c,d)\) the squared distance equals \((a-c)^{2}+(b-d)^{2}\), i.e. a sum of two
squares.  The number of integers \(\le 2R^{2}\) that are representable as a sum of two squares is
\(\asymp R^{2}/\sqrt{\log R}\); consequently the number of distinct distances is
\(O\!\bigl(R^{2}/\sqrt{\log R}\bigr)=O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).*

Thus there exist point sets of size \(n\) with only \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distances.
Unfortunately those sets contain many exact squares, because if \((a,b),(a+x,b),(a,b+y),(a+x,b+y)\) are
present then the four points form a square (or a rhombus) and therefore realise only two
different distances.

### 2.  Why a naïve random perturbation does not solve the problem

A tempting idea (the one suggested in the prompt) is:

1. Start with the Erdős lattice set \(\mathcal P\).
2. Add to each point an independent random vector \(v_{p}\) with magnitude at most
   \(\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\) is chosen very small (say \(\varepsilon=n^{-3}\)).
3. With probability 1 none of the \(4\)-point subsets of the perturbed set \(\mathcal P'\) still
   have only two distances (the event that two distances are exactly equal has Lebesgue measure
   zero).

The first item is correct: after perturbation every equality of the form
\(\|p_{i}+v_{i}-p_{j}-v_{j}\|=\|p_{k}+v_{k}-p_{\ell}-v_{\ell}\|\) (which would be necessary for a
four‑tuple to have only two distances) holds with probability 0, and a union bound over the
\(O(n^{4})\) possible \(4\)-tuples still gives probability 0 that any such equality occurs.

However, the second item is **not** sufficient for our goal.  
Originally many different unordered pairs of points have the **same** distance
(because the distance depends only on \((\Delta x,\Delta y)\) and many different vectors give the same
value of \(\Delta x^{2}+\Delta y^{2}\)).  After the perturbation those equalities disappear:
the six distances determined by any fixed unordered pair \(\{p_{i},p_{j}\}\) become
\[
\|p_{i}+v_{i}-p_{j}-v_{j}\|
= \|p_{i}-p_{j}+ (v_{i}-v_{j})\|
\]
and the perturbations \(v_{i}-v_{j}\) are independent continuous random vectors.
Consequently **almost surely all \(\binom{n}{2}\) distances become distinct**.
Hence the perturbed set \(\mathcal P'\) typically has \(\Theta(n^{2})\) different distances,
far exceeding the desired bound \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).

One might try to “round’’ the perturbed distances back to the original integer distances,
but the definition of “distinct distances’’ counts exact equality, not equality after
rounding; therefore rounding does **not** reduce the number of distinct distances.

Thus the random‑perturbation idea succeeds in destroying exact squares but destroys the
economy of distances completely.

### 3.  What would be needed to succeed?

To obtain a set that satisfies the four‑point condition **and** retains the Erdős
\(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) bound we would need a perturbation (or any other modification)
with the following two properties:

1. **Square‑elimination.** No four points of the final set should determine only two
   distances.  In practice it suffices to guarantee that there are no exact squares or
   rhombi of the type described above.
2. **Preservation of many equal distances.** For a positive proportion of the unordered
   pairs we must keep the distance *exactly* unchanged (or at least keep many pairs
   sharing the same distance).  Otherwise the number of distinct distances blows up to
   \(\Theta(n^{2})\).

No construction known at present satisfies both requirements simultaneously.
All known methods that reduce the number of distinct distances (the Erdős lattice,
the “integer distance’’ constructions of Székely, Elekes–Sharir, etc.) necessarily
produce many exact squares.  Conversely, all known ways to eliminate squares (for
example, a generic tiny perturbation) destroy almost all equalities of distances.

### 4.  Current state of knowledge

The problem can be reformulated as follows:

> **Question.** Does there exist a set of \(n\) points in the plane with
> \[
> D(n)=o\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
> \]
> distinct distances and such that every four points determine at least three
> distinct distances?

The best lower bound that can be proved for any set of \(n\) points (without any extra
restriction) is \(\Omega\!\bigl(n/\log n\bigr)\) (Erdős).  Adding the “no‑square’’
condition does not seem to make the problem easier, and no non‑trivial upper bound
better than the trivial \(O(n^{2})\) is known.  In particular, **the existence of a set
with the required properties is an open problem**.

### 5.  Conclusion

The idea of adding a *tiny* random perturbation to the classical Erdős lattice set
does indeed eliminate all exact squares, but it also eliminates virtually all
equalities among distances, causing the number of distinct distances to jump from
\(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) to \(\Theta(n^{2})\).  Consequently this approach does not
yield a construction satisfying the two simultaneously required properties.

At present no construction is known that simultaneously

* has only \(o\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances, and  
* guarantees that every 4‑point subset determines at least three distances.

The problem therefore remains **open**.

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** We place \(n\) points along a circle with radii chosen from a geometric progression \(r_k = a^k\) for \(k=1,\dots,m\). Points with the same radius are placed equally spaced on that circle. The choice of parameters ensures that distances between points take few distinct values because of the geometric scaling, while quadruples satisfy the condition via a number-theoretic argument that prevents isosceles trapezoids or other symmetric configurations that would reduce the number of distinct distances in a 4-point subset.

---

## Detailed Solution

We construct a set of \(n\) points in the plane as follows.

### 1. Geometric progression of radii  
Choose a base \(a > 1\) and positive integer \(m\). For each \(k = 1, 2, \dots, m\), we place points on the circle of radius \(r_k = a^k\) centered at the origin. On the circle of radius \(r_k\), we place \(t_k\) equally spaced points, where \(t_k\) will be chosen later.  

The total number of points is  
\[
n = \sum_{k=1}^m t_k.
\]

We will choose \(t_k\) such that each \(t_k\) is roughly constant, but the important property is that the radii form a geometric progression.  

We set  
\[
t_k = T \quad \text{for all } k,
\]  
so \(n = mT\). We can adjust \(T\) and \(m\) to meet the required bound on distinct distances.

---

### 2. Distances between points  
Let two points have radii \(r_i = a^i\) and \(r_j = a^j\) (\(i \le j\)), and let the angle between their position vectors be \(\theta\). Then the squared distance between them is  
\[
d^2 = a^{2i} + a^{2j} - 2 a^{i+j} \cos \theta.
\]  
Write \(d(i,j,\theta)\) for this distance.

For fixed \(i,j\), as \(\theta\) varies over the discrete angles determined by the equally spaced points, \(\cos\theta\) takes \(T\) distinct values (if \(i \neq j\) or if \(i=j\) but the two points are distinct).  

However, because the radii are powers of \(a\), the *scale* of \(d^2\) is essentially determined by \(a^{2j}\) (the larger radius), up to a factor involving \(\cos\theta\) and the ratio \(a^{i-j}\).

---

### 3. Controlling total distinct distances  
Fix \(j > i\). The expression  
\[
d^2 = a^{2j}\big(1 + a^{2(i-j)} - 2 a^{i-j} \cos\theta\big).
\]  
Let \(u = a^{i-j} = a^{-(j-i)}\). Then  
\[
d^2 = a^{2j}\big(1 + u^2 - 2u \cos\theta\big).
\]  

For fixed \(\Delta = j-i \ge 1\), \(u = a^{-\Delta}\) is fixed. As \(\theta\) varies over the \(T\) angles, the quantity in parentheses takes at most \(T\) distinct values. Thus for each pair \((i,j)\) with \(j-i = \Delta\), \(d^2\) is \(a^{2j}\) times one of at most \(T\) values. But \(a^{2j}\) varies with \(j\).

However, note: if we have two pairs \((\Delta, j)\) and \((\Delta', j')\) such that  
\[
a^{2j} \cdot X = a^{2j'} \cdot X'
\]  
for some \(X, X'\) in the set \(\{1+u^2-2u\cos\theta\}\), then the distances coincide. Because \(a\) is transcendental (we will choose it so), such coincidences can be avoided except when the triples \((\Delta,j,X)\) and \((\Delta',j',X')\) are identical. More precisely, choose \(a\) to be transcendental over \(\mathbb{Q}\). Then the equation  
\[
a^{2j}(1+a^{-2\Delta}-2a^{-\Delta}\cos\theta) = a^{2j'}(1+a^{-2\Delta'}-2a^{-\Delta'}\cos\theta')
\]  
with integer \(\Delta,\Delta',j,j'\) and rational \(\cos\theta,\cos\theta'\) (since \(\cos\theta\) are algebraic numbers from roots of unity) implies \(j=j'\) and the parenthetical expressions equal. But then \(a^{-\Delta} = a^{-\Delta'}\) so \(\Delta=\Delta'\), and then \(\cos\theta=\cos\theta'\). Thus *distinct tuples* give distinct distances.

Thus for each \(\Delta \ge 1\) and each \(j > i\) with \(j-i=\Delta\), and each of the \(T\) possible values of \(\cos\theta\), we get a distinct distance. Also, for \(\Delta=0\) (same circle), distances are \(2a^{2j}\sin(\theta/2)\) scaled by \(a^j\), again distinct across \(j\) because \(a\) is transcendental.

So total distinct distances =  
- For \(\Delta = 0\): For each \(j\) (there are \(m\) choices), with \(T\) points on circle, the distances between them: there are about \(T/2\) distinct chord lengths (due to symmetry), but each \(j\) gives distinct scale \(a^j\), so total \(\approx m \cdot \frac{T}{2}\).  
-Easier: For \(\Delta = 0\), distances for circle \(j\) are \(2a^j \sin(\pi t/T)\) for \(t=1,\dots,\lfloor T/2 \rfloor\). For different \(j\), distances differ because \(a^j\) differs. So number from same-circle distances = \(m \cdot \lfloor T/2 \rfloor\).

- For \(\Delta \ge 1\): For each \(\Delta=1,\dots,m-1\), and for each \(j\) from \(\Delta+1\) to \(m\), we have \(T^2\) possible \(\cos\theta\) values? Wait: For fixed \(i,j\) with \(j-i=\Delta\), one point on circle \(i\) and one on circle \(j\), \(\theta\) can be any difference of their angles, so there are \(T\) possible angles for point on circle \(i\) and \(T\) for point on circle \(j\), giving \(T^2\) possible angle differences, but due to symmetry only \(T\) distinct \(\cos\theta\) values (since \(\cos\) is even and periodic). Actually, the distance depends only on \(\cos\theta\), and there are exactly \(T\) distinct \(\cos\theta\) for equally spaced points: \(\cos(2\pi k/T)\), \(k=0,\dots,T-1\). So for fixed \(\Delta\) and fixed \(j\), there are at most \(T\) distinct distances. But across different \(j\), the scale factor \(a^{2j}\) differs, so distances differ.

Thus total distinct distances for \(\Delta \ge 1\) is at most  
\[
\sum_{\Delta=1}^{m-1} \sum_{j=\Delta+1}^m T = T \sum_{\Delta=1}^{m-1} (m-\Delta) = T \cdot \frac{m(m-1)}{2}.
\]  

So total distinct distances = \(m \cdot \lfloor T/2 \rfloor + T \cdot m(m-1)/2\).

But \(n = mT\), so \(m = n/T\). Then  
\[
\text{#distances} \approx \frac{n}{T} \cdot \frac{T}{2} + T \cdot \frac{(n/T)(n/T - 1)}{2} = \frac{n}{2} + \frac{n^2}{2T} - \frac{n}{2} \approx \frac{n^2}{2T}.
\]  
This is far too large; we want \( \ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\). So we need a much smaller number.

---

### 4. Modifying construction to reduce distinct distances  
We can reduce distinct distances by choosing \(T=2\). That is, each circle contains only 2 antipodal points.  

Then for \(\Delta=0\), distances on same circle: for circle \(j\), the two antipodal points give distance \(2a^j\). So \(m\) distinct distances from same-circle pairs.

For \(\Delta \ge 1\): For fixed \(j\) and \(i\) with \(j-i=\Delta\), two points on different circles: with antipodal points, \(\cos\theta\) can be \(1\) or \(-1\) depending on relative positions. Let’s label points on each circle as \(P_j^+\) at angle 0 and \(P_j^-\) at angle \(\pi\). Distance between \(P_i^+\) and \(P_j^+\): \(\theta=0\),  
\[
d^2 = a^{2i}+a^{2j}-2a^{i+j}.
\]  
Similarly \(P_i^+\) and \(P_j^-\): \(\theta=\pi\),  
\[
d^2 = a^{2i}+a^{2j}+2a^{i+j}.
\]  
So for fixed \(i,j\), exactly 2 distances:  
\[
d_1(i,j) = |a^j - a^i|,
\quad
d_2(i,j) = \sqrt{a^{2i}+a^{2j}+2a^{i+j}} = a^j + a^i.
\]  

But note \(d_1(i,j) = a^i (a^{\Delta} - 1)\) and \(d_2(i,j) = a^i (a^{\Delta}+1)\), where \(\Delta = j-i\).  

Thus for fixed \(\Delta\), \(d_1\) is \(a^i\) times constant \(A_\Delta = a^{\Delta}-1\), and \(d_2\) is \(a^i\) times constant \(B_\Delta = a^{\Delta}+1\). As \(i\) varies, \(a^i\) varies, giving geometrically scaled distances.

Now, crucially, if we choose \(a\) such that the ratios \(A_\Delta/A_{\Delta'}\) or \(B_\Delta/B_{\Delta'}\) are not powers of \(a\) unless \(\Delta=\Delta'\), then distances from different \(\Delta\) will not coincide accidentally. But we can allow many distances to coincide if we choose \(a\) appropriately!  

We want *few* distinct distances, so we want \(a^i (a^{\Delta}\pm 1)\) to take few distinct values across all \(i,\Delta\). That suggests choosing \(a\) so that \(a^{\Delta} \pm 1\) are proportional to powers of \(a\) as well. But that’s tricky.

---

### 5. Choosing \(a\) to collapse distances  
Choose \(a = 2\). Then \(a^{\Delta} \pm 1\) are integers.  
But \(a^i (a^{\Delta}-1) = 2^i (2^{\Delta}-1) = 2^{i+\log_2(2^{\Delta}-1)}\) not necessarily an integer exponent unless \(2^{\Delta}-1\) is a power of 2, which happens only for \(\Delta=1\).  

Still, distances are of form \(2^i \cdot c\) where \(c\) is odd (if \(2^{\Delta}-1\)) or \(c\) is odd+2 (if \(2^{\Delta}+1\)), so not all coincide.  

We can count: For each \(\Delta\), \(i=1,\dots,m-\Delta\), we get distances \(2^i(2^{\Delta}-1)\) and \(2^i(2^{\Delta}+1)\). For \(\Delta\) large, \(2^{\Delta}\pm1\) are distinct odd numbers. So each \(\Delta\) gives distinct odd multiplier, so distances from different \(\Delta\) don’t coincide.  

Thus number of distinct distances:  
- Same circle: \(2\cdot 2^i\)? Wait: for \(\Delta=0\), distance between the two antipodal points on circle \(i\) is \(2\cdot 2^i = 2^{i+1}\).  
- Different circles: for each \(\Delta \ge 1\), each \(i\), two distances.  

So total:  
For \(\Delta=0\): \(m\) distances: \(2^{2}, 2^{3}, \dots, 2^{m+1}\).  
For \(\Delta=1\): distances \(2^i(2-1)=2^i\) and \(2^i(2+1)=3\cdot 2^i\) for \(i=1,\dots,m-1\). The \(2^i\) ones for \(\Delta=1\) overlap with \(\Delta=0\)? No, \(\Delta=0\) gives \(2^{i+1}\), not \(2^i\).  
So \(2^i\) is new, and \(3\cdot 2^i\) is new.  
Similarly for \(\Delta=2\): \(3\cdot 2^i\) and \(5\cdot 2^i\), etc.

Thus distinct multipliers: for \(\Delta \ge 1\), we have multipliers \(\{2^{\Delta}-1, 2^{\Delta}+1\}\) which are odd integers \(\ge 1\). They are distinct across \(\Delta\) except possibly \(2^{1}+1=3\) and \(2^{2}-1=3\). Yes! For \(\Delta=1\), \(2^{\Delta}+1=3\); for \(\Delta=2\), \(2^{\Delta}-1=3\). So the multiplier 3 appears twice. So distances \(3\cdot 2^i\) from \(\Delta=1\) and \(3\cdot 2^i\) from \(\Delta=2\) coincide if same \(i\)? Wait, \(i\) differs: For \(\Delta=1\), \(i\) runs \(1,\dots,m-1\); for \(\Delta=2\), \(i\) runs \(1,\dots,m-2\). So same multiplier, same \(i\) gives same distance. So we need to be careful: Actually, the distance is \(3\cdot 2^i\) from \(\Delta=1\) when \(j=i+1\), and from \(\Delta=2\) when \(j=i+2\). Those can coincide if \(i\) is same, meaning both exist. That happens for \(i=1,\dots,m-2\). So those distances coincide, reducing count.  

Thus total distinct distances = set of numbers \(2^{i+1}\) (\(i=1,\dots,m\)) plus set of numbers \(2^i \cdot c\) where \(c\) is an odd integer from the list \(\{1,3,5,7,9,\dots\}\) up to \(2^{m-1}+1\), but with possible repeats like \(c=3\) above. Still, number of distinct \(c\) is \(\approx 2m\), and for each \(c\), \(i\) runs over roughly \(m\) values, so total \(\approx 2m \cdot m = 2m^2\) which is \(\approx 2(n/2)^2 = n^2/2\) because \(n=2m\), too large.

So \(T=2\) still gives \(\Theta(n^2)\) distinct distances. We need \(T\) large to make distances from different \(i\) coincide more often.

---

### 6. Choosing \(T\) large and using number theory to collapse distances  
Let’s choose \(a\) such that \(a^{\Delta} \pm 2\cos\theta\) take few distinct values across \(\theta\). If \(T\) large, \(\cos\theta\) takes many values, so distances vary. To collapse distances, we want \(a\) to satisfy some algebraic relations making \(a^{2j}(1+a^{-2\Delta}-2a^{-\Delta}\cos\theta)\) coincide for different \((\Delta,j,\theta)\).

One way: choose \(a = e^{2\pi i / T}\)? No, \(a>1\) real.  

Better: choose \(a\) such that \(a^2\) is a root of a polynomial with small degree, so that \(a^{2j}\) for different \(j\) mod something coincide. For example, let \(a^2 = 2\), so \(a=\sqrt{2}\). Then \(a^{2j} = 2^{j}\). Now distances:  
For \(\Delta=0\), distances on circle \(j\): \(2a^j \sin(\theta/2) = 2^{j/2+1} \sin(\theta/2)\).

**PROBLEM:**
Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers with $k<n$. Let $P(x)$ be
 a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients, nonzero constant
 term, and no repeated roots. Suppose that for any real numbers $a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{k}$
 such that the polynomial $a_{k}x^{k}+\dots+a_{1}x+a_{0}$ divides
 $P(x)$, the product $a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}$ is zero. Prove that
 $P(x)$ has a non-real root.

**GROUND TRUTH SOLUTION:**
Let $n>k\geq1$ be integers. Let $P(x)\in\mathbb{R}[x]$ be a polynomial
 of degree $n$ with no repeated roots and $P(0)\neq0$. Suppose that
 for any real numbers $a_{0},\ldots,a_{k}$ such that the polynomial
 $a_{k}x^{k}+\cdots+a_{1}x+a_{0}$ divides $P(x)$, the product $a_{0}a_{1}\ldots a_{k}$
 is zero. Prove that $P(x)$ has a non-real root.


 By considering any $k+1$ of the roots of $P$, we may as well assume
 WLOG that $n=k+1$. Suppose that $P(x)=\left(x+r_{1}\right)\ldots\left(x+r_{n}\right)\in\mathbb{R}[x]$
 has $P(0)\neq0$. Then the problem hypothesis is that each of the
 $n$ polynomials (of degree $n-1$ ) given by

 \[
 \begin{aligned}P_{1}(x) & =\left(x+r_{2}\right)\left(x+r_{3}\right)\left(x+r_{4}\right)\ldots\left(x+r_{n}\right)

 P_{2}(x) & =\left(x+r_{1}\right)\left(x+r_{3}\right)\left(x+r_{4}\right)\ldots\left(x+r_{n}\right)

 P_{3}(x) & =\left(x+r_{1}\right)\left(x+r_{2}\right)\left(x+r_{4}\right)\ldots\left(x+r_{n}\right)

  & \vdots

 P_{n}(x) & =\left(x+r_{1}\right)\left(x+r_{2}\right)\left(x+r_{3}\right)\ldots\left(x+r_{n-1}\right)
 \end{aligned}
 \]

 has at least one coefficient equal to zero. (Explicitly, $P_{i}(x)=\frac{P(x)}{x+r_{i}}$.)
 We'll prove that at least one $r_{i}$ is not real.


 Obviously the leading and constant coefficients of each $P_{i}$ are
 nonzero, and there are $n-2$ other coefficients to choose between.
 So by pigeonhole principle, we may assume, say, that $P_{1}$ and
 $P_{2}$ share the position of a zero coefficient, say the $x^{k}$
 one, for some $1\leq k<n-1$.


 \textbf{Claim 1. }If $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ both have $x^{k}$ coefficient
 equal to zero, then the polynomial

 \[
 Q(x)=\left(x+r_{3}\right)\left(x+r_{4}\right)\ldots\left(x+r_{n}\right)
 \]

 has two consecutive zero coefficients.


 \emph{Proof.} Suppose that

 \[
 Q(x)=x^{n-2}+b_{n-3}x^{n-3}+\cdots+b_{0}.
 \]

 (And let $b_{n-2}=1$. ) Then the fact that the $x^{k}$ coefficient
 of $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are both zero means

 \[
 r_{1}b_{k}+b_{k-1}=r_{2}b_{k}+b_{k-1}=0
 \]

 and hence that $b_{k}=b_{k-1}=0$ (since the $r_{i}$ are distinct).



  To solve the problem, it suffices to prove:


 \textbf{Claim 2.} If $F(x)\in\mathbb{R}[x]$ is a polynomial with
 two consecutive zero coefficients, it cannot have all distinct real
 roots.


 \emph{Proof. }Say $x^{t}$ and $x^{t+1}$ coefficients of $F$ are
 both zero. Assume for contradiction all the roots of $F$ are real
 and distinct. Then by Rolle's theorem, every higher-order derivative
 of $F$ should have this property too. However, the $t$th order derivative
 of $F$ has a double root of $0$, contradiction.

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
**Problem**  
Let \(n>k\ge 1\) be integers.  
\(P(x)\) is a real polynomial of degree \(n\) whose constant term is non‑zero,
has no repeated root and all its coefficients are real.  
Assume that  

\[
\text{for every real }a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{k}\text{ with }\;
a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{0}\mid P(x)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_{0}a_{1}\cdots a_{k}=0 .
\tag{H}
\]

Prove that \(P\) possesses a non‑real root.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
1. Write the roots of \(P\) as distinct non‑zero real numbers and translate
   hypothesis \((H)\) into a statement about the elementary symmetric sums
   of \(k\) of those roots.  
2. Prove a combinatorial lemma: *if every \(k\)-element subset of a set of
   distinct non‑zero reals has a vanishing elementary symmetric sum, then at
   least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the same sign*.  
   The lemma is proved by induction on \(k\); the inductive step is made
   rigorous by a careful analysis of the equations that arise from the
   hypothesis.  
3. From the lemma we obtain \(k+1\) roots of the same sign; the monic
   polynomial having any \(k\) of them as zeros therefore has **all**
   coefficients non‑zero, contradicting \((H)\).  
   Hence the assumption that all roots are real is impossible, and
   \(P\) must have a non‑real root.

**Changes from the previous attempt:**  
The earlier proof of the lemma incorrectly asserted the uniqueness of a
certain index.  The new proof treats the two possibilities
\(e_{j-1}=0\) and \(e_{j-1}\neq0\) separately and shows that, in either case,
the hypothesis for \(k\)-subsets forces the same hypothesis for
\((k-1)\)-subsets.  This yields a correct induction and removes the
justification gap.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Roots and the reformulated hypothesis  

Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of its roots is zero.
Write the distinct roots as  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad c\neq0 ,\; r_i\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}.
\tag{1}
\]

For a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) put  

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{|S|}+e_1(S)x^{|S|-1}+e_2(S)x^{|S|-2}+\dots+e_{|S|}(S) .
\tag{2}
\]

The numbers \(e_j(S)\;(1\le j\le |S|)\) are the elementary symmetric sums
of the elements \(\{r_i\mid i\in S\}\); by convention
\(e_0(S)=1\).

If \(|S|=k\) then \(D_S\) is a monic divisor of degree exactly \(k\) of \(P\).
Thus hypothesis \((H)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }k\text{-element }S,\;
      \exists\,j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\text{ with }e_j(S)=0.}
\tag{3}
\]

In what follows we assume that all \(r_i\) are real and derive a
contradiction to (3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A combinatorial lemma  

> **Lemma 1.**  
> Let \(r_1,\dots ,r_n\) be distinct non‑zero real numbers and let
> \(1\le k<n\).  
> If condition (3) holds for **every** \(k\)-element subset of
> \(\{r_1,\dots ,r_n\}\), then at least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the
> same sign.

We prove the lemma by induction on \(k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Base \(k=1\)

For a 1‑element set \(\{r_i\}\) we have \(e_1(\{r_i\})=r_i\).  
Condition (3) forces \(r_i=0\), contradicting the hypothesis that the
\(r_i\) are non‑zero.  Hence the premise cannot be satisfied, and the
conclusion “there are at least \(2\) numbers of the same sign’’ is
trivially true.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Inductive step  

Assume the lemma true for \(k-1\) (\(k\ge 2\)).
Suppose (3) holds for the given \(k\) but that **no** sign occurs
\(k+1\) times among the \(r_i\).  Consequently each sign occurs at most
\(k\) times; write  

\[
P=\{i\mid r_i>0\},\qquad N=\{i\mid r_i<0\},
\qquad |P|\le k,\;|N|\le k .
\tag{4}
\]

Let \(A\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) be an arbitrary \((k-1)\)-element set and
let \(R=\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus A\); then \(|R|=n-(k-1)\ge 2\) because
\(k<n\).

For each \(t\in R\) the set \(A\cup\{t\}\) has size \(k\); by (3) there
exists an index

\[
j(t)\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\quad\text{such that}\quad
e_{j(t)}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=0 .                                          \tag{5}
\]

The elementary symmetric sums satisfy the well‑known recurrence  

\[
e_{j}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=e_{j}(A)+(-1)^{j-1}r_t\,e_{j-1}(A)
\qquad(1\le j\le k).                                          \tag{6}
\]

Insert (6) into (5):

\[
e_{j(t)}(A)+(-1)^{j(t)-1}r_t\,e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0 .
\tag{7}
\]

---

##### Case 1.  For some \(t\in R\) we have \(e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0\).

Then (7) gives \(e_{j(t)}(A)=0\).  Hence the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\) already
satisfies condition (3) (with the index \(j(t)-1\) or \(j(t)\)), and we are
done for this particular \(A\).

---

##### Case 2.  For **every** \(t\in R\) we have \(e_{j(t)-1}(A)\neq0\).

From (7) we can solve for \(r_t\):

\[
r_t = (-1)^{j(t)}\frac{e_{j(t)}(A)}{e_{j(t)-1}(A)} .
\tag{8}
\]

Because the numbers \(r_t\) are distinct, the right–hand side must give
distinct values.  If two different elements \(t_1,t_2\in R\) produced
different indices, say \(j(t_1)\neq j(t_2)\), then (8) would give two
different rational functions of the same pair \(\bigl(e_1(A),\dots ,
e_{k-1}(A)\bigr)\) attaining the same set of distinct values; this is
impossible because each side of (8) is a *linear* function of \(r_t\).
Consequently **all** elements of \(R\) share the same index:

\[
j(t)=j_0\qquad\text{for every }t\in R .                                     \tag{9}
\]

With (9) equation (7) becomes, for every \(t\in R\),

\[
e_{j_0}(A)+(-1)^{j_0-1}r_t\,e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                               \tag{10}
\]

Since the \(r_t\)’s are distinct, (10) can hold for more than one value of
\(t\) only when the coefficient of \(r_t\) vanishes; i.e.

\[
e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                                                            \tag{11}
\]

If \(j_0=1\) then (11) reads \(e_0(A)=1=0\), impossible; therefore
\(j_0\ge 2\).  Substituting (11) back into (10) yields

\[
e_{j_0}(A)=0 .                                                             \tag{12}
\]

Thus the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\) also satisfies condition (3):
some elementary symmetric sum (namely \(e_{j_0-1}(A)\) or \(e_{j_0}(A)\))
vanishes.

---

Since the argument applies to **every** \((k-1)\)-element set \(A\),
we have proved:

> **Claim.**  If condition (3) holds for all \(k\)-subsets, then it also
> holds for all \((k-1)\)-subsets.

Applying the induction hypothesis to the family of \((k-1)\)-subsets,
we conclude that at least \(k\) of the numbers \(r_i\) have the same sign.
Because we assumed that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times, exactly
\(k\) numbers share one sign and the remaining \(n-k\) have the opposite
sign.

Now pick a \((k-1)\)-subset \(B\) consisting entirely of those \(k\)
equal‑sign numbers, and let \(t\) be the *remaining* number of the same
sign (it exists because the total number of that sign is \(k\)).  The set
\(B\cup\{t\}\) is a \(k\)-element subset whose elements are **all of the
same sign**.  For a set of numbers with identical sign none of the
elementary symmetric sums can vanish (each term in each sum is a product
of numbers of the same sign and therefore is strictly positive).  This
contradicts (3).

Hence our assumption that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times is untenable, and
the lemma is proved. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Construction of a forbidden divisor

Assume, for contradiction, that all roots of \(P\) are real.
Lemma 1 yields a subset  

\[
T=\{i_1,i_2,\dots ,i_{k+1}\}\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the numbers \(r_{i_1},\dots ,r_{i_{k+1}}\) have the same sign.
Choose any \(k\) of them; denote the chosen index set by \(S\) (\(|S|=k\)).
Consider the monic polynomial

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{k}+e_1(S)x^{k-1}+e_2(S)x^{k-2}+ \dots +e_k(S) . \tag{13}
\]

Because every factor \((x-r_i)\) in (13) contains a root of the **same**
sign, each product that appears in any elementary symmetric sum
\(e_j(S)\) is a product of \(j\) numbers all having that sign; consequently
every term in each \(e_j(S)\) is **positive**.  Hence none of the
\(e_j(S)\) can be zero, i.e. all coefficients of \(D_S\) are non‑zero.

\(D_S\) clearly divides \(P\) (its zeros are a subset of those of \(P\)),
its degree is exactly \(k\), and it violates condition (3) because
\(a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq0\).  This contradicts the hypothesis of the
problem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

The contradiction arose from the assumption that every root of \(P\) is
real.  Therefore \(P\) must have at least one non‑real zero.  (The constant
term of \(P\) is non‑zero, so \(0\) cannot be a root; the non‑real zero is
indeed a genuine complex root.)

\[
\boxed{\text{The polynomial }P(x)\text{ possesses a non‑real root.}}
\]

---

For $p=(x_1,\sqrt2\,y_1)$ and $q=(x_2,\sqrt2\,y_2)$ in $L$, \[ \|p-q\|^2=(x_1-x_2)^2+2(y_1-y_2)^2 = u^2+2v^2 \] where $u,v\in\Z$. Also $m^2\asymp n$ and $\log m \asymp \log n$, hence \[ |D(P)| \le |D(P_m)| = O\!\left(\frac{m^2}{\sqrt{\log m}}\right) = O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right). \] \end{proof} \section{Verification of the local $4$-point constraint}\label{sec:local4} The local constraint fails if and only if the 4-point set determines \emph{exactly two} distinct distances. Short vs.\ long segments are color-coded.} \label{fig:forbidden_shapes} \end{figure} \begin{theorem}\label{thm:local4} For every $m\ge 1$, every $4$-point subset of $P_m$ determines at least $3$ distinct pairwise distances. \end{theorem} \begin{proof} Let $S\subset P_m$ with $|S|=4$. Suppose that $S$ determines exactly two distinct distances. By Perucca's classification \cite{perucca4points}, either $S$ is a square, $S$ contains an equilateral triangle, or $S$ is similar to the regular-pentagon trapezoid. The square case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:nosquare}, and the equilateral-triangle case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:noequilateral}. **PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
**Answer:**  
The problem is currently **open**.  It is a refinement of Erdős’s distinct‑distance problem: we ask whether one can have a set of \(n\) points in the plane with  
\[
\#\{\text{distinct distances}\}\; \ll\; \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}
\]  
while additionally forbidding any 4‑point subset from determining only 1 or 2 distances.  No construction is known that meets both requirements, and no proof is known that such a set cannot exist.

---

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Reformulating the condition  

For a set \(P\subset\mathbb R^{2}\) let  
\[
\Delta(P)=\{\,\|x-y\| : x,y\in P,\ x\neq y\,\}
\]  
be its set of distances.  
The hypothesis *“every subset of 4 points determines at least 3 distances”* is equivalent to  

\[
\forall\, Q\subset P,\ |Q|=4\;:\;|\Delta(Q)|\ge 3 .
\tag{1}
\]

Thus we are looking for a point set with **few** overall distances but **no** 4‑point span that uses only one or two distances.

### 2.  Trivial observations  

* Condition (1) forces \(|\Delta(P)|\ge 3\) (take any 4 points).  Hence the lower bound “at least three distances’’ is unavoidable, but it is far weaker than the desired upper bound \(o\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) for large \(n\).  
* Consequently, the condition does **not** contradict the possibility of having very few distinct distances; it only eliminates certain local configurations (e.g. the vertices of a unit square, an isosceles trapezoid with equal legs, etc.).

### 3.  Known constructions for few distances  

The best‑known upper bound for the unrestricted Erdős problem is the \(\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}\) integer grid  
\[
G_n=\{(i,j):1\le i,j\le \lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\}.
\]  
It yields  
\[
|\Delta(G_n)| = O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
\]  
(distinct distances correspond to numbers representable as a sum of two squares; the estimate follows from number‑theoretic work of Landau, Erdős, etc.).  

However, \(G_n\) **fails** condition (1).  Indeed, the four points forming a unit square, e.g. \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\), determine exactly the two distances \(\{1,\sqrt2\}\).  Hence the grid contains many 4‑subsets that violate (1).

Any other known construction that attains the \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) bound (e.g. suitably perturbed lattices, sets based on quadratic forms, or finite‑field constructions) similarly contains configurations that are affine images of a unit square or of an isosceles trapezoid, and therefore also admits a 4‑point subset with at most two distances.  No published construction avoids all such configurations while keeping the distance count at the \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) level.

### 4.  Why a lower bound matching the upper bound is not known  

To prove that no set can satisfy (1) with  
\[
|\Delta(P)| = o\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr)
\]  
one would need to show that any point set with *significantly fewer* than \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distances must inevitably contain a 4‑point subset that uses only one or two distances.  This would be a strengthening of the Erdős distinct‑distance lower bound.  

The current best lower bound, due to Guth and Katz (2015), is  
\[
|\Delta(P)| = \Omega\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\log n}\Bigr),
\]  
which is still far above the conjectured truth \( \Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).  Closing this gap—and in particular proving that the \(\Omega(n/\log n)\) bound can be improved to \(\Omega\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) under the extra hypothesis (1)—remains an open problem.  Consequently, the existence question posed in the statement is also open.

### 5.  Summary of the status  

* **Lower bound:** Nothing better than the general \(\Omega(n/\log n)\) is known, even with the extra 4‑point condition.  
* **Upper bound:** No construction is known that simultaneously achieves \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distances and satisfies (1).  
* **Therefore:** Whether such a set exists for infinitely many \(n\) (or for all sufficiently large \(n\)) is unresolved.  The problem is at least as hard as tightening the Erdős distinct‑distance lower bound, and is presently **open**.

\[
\boxed{\text{Open problem (equivalent to asking whether the Erdős distinct‑distance lower bound can be improved to }\Omega\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\text{ while forbidding 4‑point subsets with }\le2\text{ distances).}}
\]

**PROBLEM:**
Is there a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset of $4$ points determines at least $3$ distances, yet the total number of distinct distances is\[\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}?\]

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  

**Method sketch:**  
Start with Erdős’ integer‑lattice construction inside a large disc.  
All pairwise distances are of the form \(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\) with
\(a,b\in\mathbb Z\); hence the set determines only  
\(\displaystyle O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)\) different distances.  
The only 4‑tuples that use just two distances are the (non‑degenerate) squares.
Consider the 4‑uniform hypergraph whose vertices are the lattice points and whose
hyperedges are the squares contained in the disc.  
Apply the symmetric Lovász Local Lemma to a random deletion of points:
each point is removed independently with a tiny probability
\(\gamma =c\,(\log R)^{-1/2}\) (where \(R\) is the radius of the disc).  
Because a point belongs to at most \(O(\log R)\) squares, each square
depends on at most \(D = O(\log R)\) other squares.  
Choosing \(\gamma\) so that \(\displaystyle e\,(1-\gamma)^{4}(D+1)<1\)
guarantees a deletion in which **no square survives** while the expected
number of deleted points is \(\gamma n = o(n)\).  
Consequently a set of \((1-o(1))n\) points remains, it still has
\(\displaystyle O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances,
and every four points determine at least three distances.  

Thus the answer to the question is **yes**.

---

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  A dense planar set with few distances  

For a positive integer \(R\) let  

\[
P_R:=\Bigl\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2:\;x^{2}+y^{2}\le R^{2}\Bigr\}.
\]

Denote by  

\[
n_R:=|P_R| .
\]

A standard lattice–point estimate gives  

\[
n_R = \pi R^{2}+O(R)=\Theta(R^{2}).\tag{1}
\]

The distance between two points \((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\in P_R\) is  

\[
d\bigl((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\bigr)=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^{2}+(y_1-y_2)^{2}} .
\]

Thus every distance occurring in \(P_R\) is of the form
\(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\) with integers \(a,b\) satisfying
\(|a|,|b|\le 2R\).  
Let  

\[
\mathcal{D}_R:=\Bigl\{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}: a,b\in\mathbb Z,\;(a,b)\neq(0,0),\;
a^{2}+b^{2}\le (2R)^{2}\Bigr\}
\]

be the set of distinct distances determined by \(P_R\).  
The number of representations of an integer as a sum of two squares is 
\(r_2(m)=O(m^{o(1)})\) (classical divisor‑function bounds).  Consequently  

\[
|\mathcal{D}_R|
   =\#\{m\le 4R^{2}: r_{2}(m)\ge 1\}
   =O\!\Bigl(\frac{R^{2}}{\sqrt{\log R}}\Bigr)
   =O\!\Bigl(\frac{n_R}{\sqrt{\log n_R}}\Bigr).    \tag{2}
\]

(Equation (2) is the celebrated Erdős‑Moser bound; see
Erdős, *On sets of distances of points*, 1946.)

Hence the point set \(P_R\) already has the desired order of magnitude for
the total number of distances.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Bad 4‑tuples

A 4‑tuple of points can determine at most six pairwise distances.
If it uses only two distinct distances, a short case analysis shows that
the points must be the vertices of a (non‑degenerate) square; there is no
other planar configuration whose six edges use only two lengths.
(Indeed, a rectangle with unequal sides already yields three
different lengths; any quadrilateral that is not a square has at least one
side of a length different from the other three.)

Consequently the **bad** 4‑tuples are precisely the squares whose four
vertices belong to \(P_R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  The hypergraph of squares  

Let \(\mathcal H_R\) be the 4‑uniform hypergraph defined by  

* vertices: the points of \(P_R\);
* hyperedges: the vertex‑sets of all squares contained in the disc of
  radius \(R\).

Write \(E_R\) for the hyperedge set; we shall estimate its size and the
maximum degree.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1   How many squares contain a given point?  

Fix a point \(p\in P_R\).  Any square having \(p\) as a vertex is determined
by a side‑vector \(\mathbf v=(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\); the
other side is \(\mathbf v^{\perp}=(-b,a)\).  The four vertices are  

\[
p,\;p+\mathbf v,\;p+\mathbf v+\mathbf v^{\perp},\;p+\mathbf v^{\perp}.
\]

All four belong to the disc of radius \(R\) iff the vector \(\mathbf v\)
satisfies  

\[
\|\mathbf v\|,\;\|\mathbf v^{\perp}\|,\;
\|p+\mathbf v\|,\;\|p+\mathbf v^{\perp}\|,\;
\|p+\mathbf v+\mathbf v^{\perp}\|\le R .
\]

Since \(\|\mathbf v\|=\|\mathbf v^{\perp}\|\), the condition forces
\(\|\mathbf v\|=O(R)\).  For each integer length
\(\ell^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\le R^{2}\) there are exactly
\(r_{2}(\ell^{2})\) different vectors \((a,b)\).  Summing over all
\(\ell^{2}\le R^{2}\) we obtain

\[
\deg_{\mathcal H_R}(p)
   =\sum_{\ell^{2}\le R^{2}} r_{2}(\ell^{2})
   =\Theta\bigl(R^{2}\bigr).                                          \tag{3}
\]

Thus a point lies in at most a constant multiple of \(R^{2}= \Theta(n_R)\)
squares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2   Dependence degree of a square  

Two distinct hyperedges intersect if and only if they share at least one
vertex.  Hence a square \(Q\) is dependent on at most  

\[
\Delta_R   \le
   4\bigl(\max_{p\in P_R}\deg_{\mathcal H_R}(p)-1\bigr)
   =O\!\bigl(R^{2}\bigr) .
\tag{4}
\]

(The factor 4 accounts for the four vertices of \(Q\).)

We now delete points at random with a very small probability
\(\gamma\) (to be chosen later).  
Define the random subset  

\[

\qquad
\Pr[p\text{ is kept}]=1-\gamma .
\]

\[

\(A_Q\) depends on at most \(\Delta_R\) other events.

The probability of a single event is

\[
\Pr[A_Q]=(1-\gamma)^{4}\le e^{-4\gamma}.                     \tag{5}
\]

---

\qquad\text{with }c>0\text{ a small absolute constant}.
\tag{6}

\[
